stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, comparing three Afro-Eurasian trade networks, c. 1200–1450
stimulusBlocks.text:
The Silk Roads, the Indian Ocean, and the trans-Saharan routes are often taught as separate systems, but merchants and goods moved among them. Gold from West Africa crossed the Sahara to North African and Egyptian markets that also traded with the Indian Ocean. Chinese porcelain reached East African ports by sea, while Chinese silk moved west by both land and sea.

What distinguished the networks was less what they connected than how. Desert crossings depended on camels, oases, and the knowledge of guides; maritime routes depended on the monsoon calendar and port cities where ships waited for the winds to change. These conditions shaped which goods traveled, which cities grew, and which rulers could profit.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, why did different cities grow on different networks?
choices: Cities grew only in the places where Mongol rulers founded new capitals
Transport needs mattered less than the question of which rulers controlled the most gold
Cities grew wherever merchants who traveled from Europe chose to settle down
Transport needs, such as oases or ports for waiting ships, shaped where cities rose
questions.explanation: The passage links desert oases and monsoon ports to which cities and rulers could profit.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 2.7 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: The passage does not attribute city growth to Mongol capitals.
The passage emphasizes transport conditions, not gold alone.
The passage does not discuss European settlement.
The passage links desert oases and monsoon ports to which cities and rulers could profit.
questions.distinguisher: Use the passage's explanation: conditions of travel.

stimulusBlocks.attribution: Marco Polo, Venetian merchant who traveled in Mongol-ruled Asia c. 1271–1295, account dictated to the writer Rustichello of Pisa, c. 1298, describing the Malabar coast of southwestern India
stimulusBlocks.citation: The Book of Ser Marco Polo, trans. Henry Yule, rev. Henri Cordier, 3rd ed. (London: John Murray, 1903), vol. 2, Book III, ch. 25. Project Gutenberg eBook #12410.
stimulusBlocks.note: Melibar is Malabar; Gozurat is Gujarat; Manzi is southern China.
stimulusBlocks.text:
And you must know that from this kingdom of Melibar, and from another near it called Gozurat, there go forth every year more than a hundred corsair vessels on cruize. . . . But now the merchants are aware of this, and go so well manned and armed, and with such great ships, that they don't fear the corsairs. . . .

Ships come hither from many quarters, but especially from the great province of Manzi. Coarse spices are exported hence both to Manzi and to the west, and that which is carried by the merchants to Aden goes on to Alexandria, but the ships that go in the latter direction are not one to ten of those that go to the eastward

stimulusBlocks.attribution: Ibn Battuta, Muslim legal scholar from Morocco who traveled c. 1325–1354, account dictated to the writer Ibn Juzayy, 1355, describing his journey south across the Sahara toward Mali, 1352
stimulusBlocks.citation: Ibn Battuta, Travels in Asia and Africa, 1325–1354, trans. H. A. R. Gibb (London: George Routledge & Sons, 1929), ch. 14. Checked against Internet Archive scan travelsinasiaafr0000ibnb, scan p. 339.
stimulusBlocks.note: Bracketed words replace the translator's dated terms for West Africa and West Africans. Sijilmasa was a Moroccan caravan city; the Massufa were a Berber group.
stimulusBlocks.text: After twenty-five days we reached Taghaza, an unattractive village, with the curious feature that its houses and mosques are built of blocks of salt, roofed with camel skins. There are no trees there, nothing but sand. In the sand is a salt mine; they dig for the salt, and find it in thick slabs, lying one on top of the other, as though they had been tool-squared and laid under the surface of the earth. . . . A camel will carry two of these slabs. No one lives at Taghaza except the slaves of the Massufa tribe, who dig for the salt; they subsist on dates imported from Dar'a and Sijilmasa, camels' flesh, and millet imported from [West Africa]. [West Africans] come up from their country and take away the salt from there.

questions.explanation: Each network had its own dangers: corsairs at sea, and in the desert, food imported from far away.

stimulusBlocks.attribution: Marco Polo, Venetian merchant who traveled in Mongol-ruled Asia c. 1271–1295, account dictated to the writer Rustichello of Pisa, c. 1298, describing the port of Quanzhou in southern China
stimulusBlocks.citation: The Book of Ser Marco Polo, trans. Henry Yule, rev. Henri Cordier, 3rd ed. (London: John Murray, 1903), vol. 2, Book II, ch. 82. Project Gutenberg eBook #12410.
stimulusBlocks.note: Zayton is Quanzhou. “The Great Kaan” is Kublai Khan. Christendom means Christian Europe.
stimulusBlocks.text:
At this city you must know is the Haven of Zayton, frequented by all the ships of India, which bring thither spicery and all other kinds of costly wares. . . . And I assure you that for one shipload of pepper that goes to Alexandria or elsewhere, destined for Christendom, there come a hundred such, aye and more too, to this haven of Zayton; for it is one of the two greatest havens in the world for commerce.

The Great Kaan derives a very large revenue from the duties paid in this city and haven; for you must know that on all the merchandize imported, including precious stones and pearls, he levies a duty of ten per cent., or in other words takes tithe of everything.

stimulusBlocks.attribution: Ibn Battuta, Muslim legal scholar from Morocco who traveled c. 1325–1354, account dictated to the writer Ibn Juzayy, 1355, describing his stay in the Mali Empire, 1352–1353
stimulusBlocks.citation: Ibn Battuta, Travels in Asia and Africa, 1325–1354, trans. H. A. R. Gibb (London: George Routledge & Sons, 1929), ch. 14. Checked against Internet Archive scan travelsinasiaafr0000ibnb, scan pp. 351–352.
stimulusBlocks.note: Bracketed words replace the translator's dated term for West Africans. “White men” refers to North African and Arab visitors and merchants.
stimulusBlocks.text:
[The people of Mali] possess some admirable qualities. They are seldom unjust, and have a greater abhorrence of injustice than any other people. Their sultan shows no mercy to anyone who is guilty of the least act of it. There is complete security in their country. Neither traveller nor inhabitant in it has anything to fear from robbers or men of violence. They do not confiscate the property of any white man who dies in their country, even if it be uncounted wealth. On the contrary, they give it into the charge of some trustworthy person among the whites, until the rightful heir takes possession of it. They are careful to observe the hours of prayer, and assiduous in attending them in congregations, and in bringing up their children to them. . . .

Yet another is their zeal for learning the Koran by heart. . . . Among their bad qualities are the following. . . . Then there is their custom of putting dust and ashes on their heads, as a mark of respect, and the grotesque ceremonies we have described when the poets recite their verses.

stimulusBlocks.attribution: Marco Polo, Venetian merchant who traveled in Mongol-ruled Asia c. 1271–1295, account dictated to the writer Rustichello of Pisa, c. 1298, describing the port of Quanzhou in southern China
stimulusBlocks.citation: The Book of Ser Marco Polo, trans. Henry Yule, rev. Henri Cordier, 3rd ed. (London: John Murray, 1903), vol. 2, Book II, ch. 82. Project Gutenberg eBook #12410.
stimulusBlocks.note: Zayton is Quanzhou. “The Great Kaan” is Kublai Khan. Christendom means Christian Europe.
stimulusBlocks.text:
At this city you must know is the Haven of Zayton, frequented by all the ships of India, which bring thither spicery and all other kinds of costly wares. . . . And I assure you that for one shipload of pepper that goes to Alexandria or elsewhere, destined for Christendom, there come a hundred such, aye and more too, to this haven of Zayton; for it is one of the two greatest havens in the world for commerce.

The Great Kaan derives a very large revenue from the duties paid in this city and haven; for you must know that on all the merchandize imported, including precious stones and pearls, he levies a duty of ten per cent., or in other words takes tithe of everything.

stimulusBlocks.attribution: Ibn Battuta, Muslim legal scholar from Morocco who traveled c. 1325–1354, account dictated to the writer Ibn Juzayy, 1355, describing his stay in the Mali Empire, 1352–1353
stimulusBlocks.citation: Ibn Battuta, Travels in Asia and Africa, 1325–1354, trans. H. A. R. Gibb (London: George Routledge & Sons, 1929), ch. 14. Checked against Internet Archive scan travelsinasiaafr0000ibnb, scan pp. 351–352.
stimulusBlocks.note: Bracketed words replace the translator's dated term for West Africans. “White men” refers to North African and Arab visitors and merchants.
stimulusBlocks.text:
[The people of Mali] possess some admirable qualities. They are seldom unjust, and have a greater abhorrence of injustice than any other people. Their sultan shows no mercy to anyone who is guilty of the least act of it. There is complete security in their country. Neither traveller nor inhabitant in it has anything to fear from robbers or men of violence. They do not confiscate the property of any white man who dies in their country, even if it be uncounted wealth. On the contrary, they give it into the charge of some trustworthy person among the whites, until the rightful heir takes possession of it. They are careful to observe the hours of prayer, and assiduous in attending them in congregations, and in bringing up their children to them. . . .

Yet another is their zeal for learning the Koran by heart. . . . Among their bad qualities are the following. . . . Then there is their custom of putting dust and ashes on their heads, as a mark of respect, and the grotesque ceremonies we have described when the poets recite their verses.
